title: The Growth of Nationalism and the Early Nationalists
tagline: Why the idea of a nation took hold in India: factors, early leaders and the founding of the Congress.

overview.intro: Nationalism did not arrive in India with a single speech; it grew out of the very changes that colonial rule made — railways and print, English education, the unification of administration, the economic grievances of peasants and artisans, and the rediscovery of India’s own past. This chapter sets out the factors that made a common Indian identity thinkable, the early leaders who gave it institutions and a vocabulary, and the founding of the Indian National Congress in 1885 with its early programme of petitions and prayers. The examiner’s two standard questions are the factors question, marked by head, and the question on the early nationalists, marked by leader and contribution.

facts.label: Factor: unity
facts.value: The unification of the country under one administration, one army, one postal system and one network of railways and telegraphs.

facts.label: Factor: education
facts.value: English education and the press gave Indians a common language in which to address one another across regions.

facts.label: The early leaders
facts.value: Ranade, Gokhale, Dadabhai Naoroji, Surendranath Banerjee and W. C. Bonnerjee gave the movement its method and its statistics.

Describe the contribution of at least four early leaders of the national movement.

Distinguish between the Moderates and the Extremists on method, though the detailed comparison belongs to the next chapter.

learn.title: The factors that gave rise to nationalism

blocks.text: The factors divide neatly into five heads, each of which deserves an instance. Political: the British unified the country under a single government, ended the multiplicity of quarrelling states and introduced equal law and a single system of administration, but their own record of conquest, annexation and the arbitrary treatment of princes gave Indians a common grievance to match the common administration. Economic: the drain of wealth, the destruction of Indian industry by British manufactures and the burden of land revenue convinced economists such as Dadabhai Naoroji that India’s poverty was not natural but produced by policy, and shared economic distress is a powerful maker of solidarity. Social and religious: reform movements such as the Brahmo Samaj and the Arya Samaj removed social evils, spread education and encouraged Indians to think of themselves as one people with a shared heritage. Educational: English gave a common language to the educated, and the study of European history and of India’s own classics supplied the models and the memories of nationhood. Administrative and technological: railways, the telegraph, the postal system, newspapers and a common legal system made travel, news and organised activity possible across the subcontinent for the first time.

items: Political unity and equal law under one administration, set against British conquests and annexations that supplied the grievance.
Economic: the drain of wealth, the ruin of industry and the land revenue burden, as demonstrated by Dadabhai Naoroji.
Social and religious reform: the Brahmo Samaj, the Arya Samaj and similar movements removed evils and fostered a shared identity.
Education and the press: English plus newspapers such as The Hindu, Kesari and Amrita Bazar Patrika carried ideas across regions.
Administrative improvements: railways, telegraph, postal system and a uniform legal system made all-India unity practicable.
The study of European history and of India’s past supplied the vocabulary of liberty, nationalism and self-government.

blocks.caption: Factors behind the rise of nationalism
rows: One administration and equal law, but annexation and disrespect to princes created common grievance
Drain of wealth and ruin of industry gave economists a shared case against colonial rule
Reform movements removed evils and fostered pride in a shared heritage
English and European political thought supplied the language and the models
Railways, telegraph and press made all-India organisation possible

items.note: Dadabhai Naoroji’s calculation that a large part of India’s revenues left the country as home charges turned an abstract grievance into a statistic that every newspaper could repeat.
A speech delivered in Bengali could be carried in English to Madras and Bombay within a week, which is why a common language mattered as much as the ideas themselves.

items.meaning: The idea that people sharing a territory, history and culture form one nation with the right to govern themselves.
The transfer of Indian revenues to Britain through salaries, pensions and home charges, first quantified by Dadabhai Naoroji.
Newspapers and journals that carried political discussion across regions and built an all-India public opinion.
Movements against caste oppression, child marriage and other evils that also fostered a sense of common nationhood.

learn.title: The early leaders and their contribution

blocks.text: The generation before the Congress gave nationalism its method, its statistics and its institutions. Mahadev Govind Ranade of the Poona Deshasteshi Sabha preached constructive work and economic regeneration and argued that political advance must rest on social reform. Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Ranade’s disciple, founded the Deccan Education Society and the Fergusson College and later led the moderate wing, insisting on constitutional methods and gradual reform. Dadabhai Naoroji, the Grand Old Man of India, founded the East India Association, sat in the House of Commons for Finsbury, and through Poverty and Un-British Rule in India developed the drain theory that gave nationalists their central economic argument. Surendranath Banerjee founded the Indian National Conference in 1883 and the Indian National Association in 1885, started a chain of schools and the newspaper The Bengalee, and built the network of petitions and conferences that fed the first session of the Congress. Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee, a barrister from Bengal, became the first President of the Congress in 1885. Together these leaders established the practice of annual sessions, the discipline of debating and petitioning, and the belief that Indians could conduct their own political business.

items: M. G. Ranade: the Poona Deshasteshi Sabha and the twin programme of social reform and economic regeneration.
G. K. Gokhale: the Deccan Education Society and Fergusson College; the model of patient constitutional agitation.
Dadabhai Naoroji: the East India Association, MP for Finsbury, and the drain theory of Poverty and Un-British Rule in India.
Surendranath Banerjee: the Indian National Conference of 1883, the Indian National Association of 1885, The Bengalee and a chain of schools.
W. C. Bonnerjee: the first President of the Indian National Congress, 1885.
Annie Besant and other theosophists and lecturers spread the idea of self-rule through societies and public meetings.

items.note: As an elected member of the House of Commons he could put the Indian case in the heart of British politics, which no petition from India could match.
By running schools and a newspaper he built the constituency of educated Indians that the Congress would later mobilise.

learn.title: The founding of the Indian National Congress

blocks.text: The Congress was founded in December 1885 at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay, with thirty-two delegates and W. C. Bonnerjee in the chair. The idea had more than one parent: A. O. Hume, a retired civil servant, brought the delegates together and served as its first general secretary; Surendranath Banerjee’s Indian National Association had already shown that an all-India body was possible; and the Indian League and the National Indian Association had kept the demand for a share in government alive. The immediate prompt was the Ilbert Bill controversy, which showed how easily official goodwill could be withdrawn, and the Vernacular Press Act, which had demonstrated the power of the state against the Indian press. The Congress adopted a cautious method: it met once a year, passed resolutions, submitted memorials and petitions and trained Indians in parliamentary procedure, with an early programme demanding Indians in the higher services, the reduction of military expenditure, the reform of the council system and greater representation for Indians in the councils. Its significance lies less in what it won than in what it was — a forum in which Bengalis, Punjabis, Maharashtrians and Tamils sat together and thought of themselves as Indians before they thought of their regions.

items: Founded in December 1885 at Bombay; thirty-two delegates; W. C. Bonnerjee the first President and A. O. Hume the first general secretary.
Precursors: the Indian League, the Indian National Association and Surendranath Banerjee’s National Conference.
Immediate triggers: the Ilbert Bill controversy, the Vernacular Press Act and disappointment with the council reforms.
Early method: annual sessions, resolutions, memorials and petitions — the prayer, petition and protest approach.
Early programme: Indians in the higher services, reduction of military expenditure, reformed councils and wider representation.
Significance: an all-India forum that cut across region, language and community and trained leaders in constitutional politics.

blocks.caption: The first session of the Congress, 1885
rows: Resolutions, memorials and petitions, with no confrontation

items.note: The bill sought to allow Indian magistrates to try Europeans, and the official reversal under pressure showed educated Indians how little weight their status carried, which made an all-India body look necessary.
A delegate who had never left his province sat with a delegate from Madras and discovered that their grievances and hopes were much the same — the intangible achievement of the early sessions.

learn.title: Why the early Congress petitioned, and what it achieved

blocks.text: It is easy to mock the early Congress for its loyalty and its memorials, but the method followed from the analysis its leaders had made. The British had granted councils and promised reforms whenever they needed Indian support, so the nationalists calculated that evidence, statistics and reasoned memorials would be cheaper and safer than agitation in a country where the government had overwhelming force and where Indians had no arms, no money and no press freedom. The method also suited their social base: professionals, lawyers and landowners who had something to lose from disorder. Its achievements were accordingly institutional rather than legislative: the Congress kept the demand for self-government continuously before the rulers, created a national leadership, established the habit of annual deliberation across regions, and produced the statistics — the drain, the deindustrialisation, the budget analysis — that made colonial rule arguable rather than merely accepted. Its limitations were equally real: it was a body of the educated and the well-to-do, it worked within the law and could not therefore challenge the law itself, and its caution left peasants and workers outside. Those limits explain the rise of the Extremists after 1905 and the mass politics that followed 1919.

items: The method of petition followed from a calculation of strength: no arms and no mass base, but facts, statistics and constitutional argument.
The Congress kept the demand for a share in government continuously alive through annual sessions and memorials.
It built an all-India leadership and the practice of deliberating across regions, languages and communities.
Its economists supplied the arguments: the drain of wealth, the ruin of industry and the analysis of the budget.
Its limitations: an elite social base, reliance on the goodwill of the ruler, and no mass participation.

items.note: A memorial quoting the drain of wealth in figures gave an official something to answer, whereas an unsupported demand could simply be filed away.
Because the Congress would not break the law, it could ask for reforms but could not mobilise the millions who had no vote, no property and no access to a petition.

questions.prompt: The Indian National Congress was founded in the year:
questions.explanation: The first session met in Bombay in December 1885 with thirty-two delegates.

questions.prompt: The first President of the Indian National Congress was:
questions.explanation: Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee presided over the first session; Hume was the general secretary.

questions.prompt: The drain of wealth theory was developed by:
questions.explanation: Dadabhai Naoroji set out the drain theory in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India.

questions.prompt: Which organisation was founded by Surendranath Banerjee in 1885?
questions.explanation: Surendranath Banerjee founded the Indian National Association in 1885, after the Indian National Conference of 1883.

questions.prompt: The Congress met once a year, and its gatherings were called annual __________.
questions.explanation: The annual session became the institution through which nationalists trained themselves in debate and resolution-making.

questions.prompt: The __________ Samaj, founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy, removed social evils and fostered a sense of common heritage.
questions.explanation: The Brahmo Samaj and the Arya Samaj are the reform movements most often named as social factors behind nationalism.

questions.prompt: Explain how English education contributed to the rise of nationalism.
questions.answer: English education gave Indians across the regions a common language in which to address one another, so a leader from Bengal could read and answer an argument printed in Madras. It also carried European political ideas — liberty, equality, representative government and the rights of nations — which supplied both the vocabulary and the models for demanding a share in government. Finally, it produced the class of lawyers, teachers and journalists who had the skills and the confidence to organise petitions, newspapers and an annual national session.
questions.explanation: A common language, the ideas it carried and the professional class it produced are the three strands of the answer.

questions.prompt: State three economic factors that contributed to the growth of nationalism.
questions.answer: First, the drain of wealth, calculated by Dadabhai Naoroji, showed that a large part of Indian revenues left the country for Britain. Second, the ruin of Indian handicrafts and textiles by machine-made British goods threw artisans out of work and impoverished the countryside. Third, the land revenue demand, often raised at resettlement and exacted through moneylenders, burdened the peasant while exports and taxation enriched the metropolitan economy. These shared grievances gave the educated, the artisan and the peasant a common economic case against colonial rule.
questions.explanation: The drain, deindustrialisation and the revenue burden are the three economic heads the marking scheme expects.

questions.prompt: Mention two organisations founded by early nationalist leaders before the Congress.
questions.answer: The East India Association was founded by Dadabhai Naoroji in 1866 to place Indian views before the British public, and the Indian National Association was founded by Surendranath Banerjee in 1885 to bring together delegates from all parts of the country. The Poona Deshasteshi Sabha, founded by M. G. Ranade, and the Deccan Education Society of G. K. Gokhale are further instances.
questions.explanation: Any two of the East India Association, Indian National Association, Poona Deshasteshi Sabha, Deccan Education Society and Indian League will do.

questions.prompt: Describe the political, administrative and educational factors that led to the rise of nationalism in India.
questions.answer: Politically, the British unified the country under a single government after ending the multiplicity of warring states and introduced a uniform law, so Indians for the first time lived under one administration; at the same time their record of conquest, the Doctrine of Lapse, the annexation of Awadh and the treatment of princes gave these varied groups a common grievance. Administratively, railways, the telegraph, the postal system and the printed press linked the provinces and made it possible to carry news and to organise all-India conferences within a few days, while a single legal system gave every subject the same remedies and a common vocabulary of rights. Educationally, English became the language of the higher administration and of the educated, and through it Indians read European histories of liberty and self-government as well as their own classical literature, which gave them both the models of the nation and pride in their own heritage. The press multiplied the effect: newspapers in English and the vernacular carried debates on the drain of wealth, the Ilbert Bill and the Vernacular Press Act into every reading household, turning separate grievances into a shared public opinion.
questions.explanation: Each head needs definition, mechanism and instance, and the answer should end by showing how the three heads reinforced one another.

questions.prompt: Why did the early Congress confine itself to petitions and memorials instead of agitation?
questions.answer: The method followed from an honest calculation of resources. Indians had no arms, no mass organisation and no funds, while the government possessed an army, an efficient civil service and the power to imprison or ban any body it disliked, so a challenge of force would have been crushed and would have lost the gains already made. The leadership itself came from lawyers, landowners and professionals whose security and careers depended on lawful conduct, and who believed that a case supported by statistics — the drain of wealth, the military budget, the unemployed graduates — was more persuasive to a parliament that read such arguments than a demonstration that could be dismissed as disorder. The constitutional method also kept the doors of the councils open: the British had repeatedly promised reforms, and the nationalists calculated that loyal cooperation would win concessions that agitation would forfeit. The limits of this reasoning were real, since the petitions produced few concrete results and left peasants and workers outside politics, but at the stage when the Congress had no mass base it was the method that both the situation and the membership allowed.
questions.explanation: The balance of forces, the social composition of the leadership and the expectation of concessions together explain the petition method, and the answer should also note where the reasoning failed.

questions.prompt: Did the early Indian National Congress represent all sections of Indian society? Give reasons and state the consequences of its limitations.
questions.answer: It did not. The Congress of 1885 and the decades that followed were drawn from a narrow social base: lawyers, teachers, journalists, merchants and landowners who knew English, could afford the fare to an annual session and had the leisure to discuss politics, and its sessions, resolutions and memorials were conducted in a language and a procedure that the peasant, the artisan and the industrial worker could not enter. Women were present at public meetings but were not part of the decision-making of the early sessions, and the Depressed Classes and the industrial proletariat had no voice in a body that spoke in the name of India as a whole. The consequences were structural rather than accidental: because the base was narrow, the method had to be constitutional, since petitions require a petitioner and a receptive reader; because it was constitutional, the concrete gains were few, which is exactly what pushed the Assertives into swadeshi and boycott after 1905; and because the masses were outside, the Congress could be treated by the government as a debating society until Gandhi organised the villages and the towns into the movements after 1919. The balanced judgement is therefore that the early Congress created the platform and the vocabulary of nationalism but could not yet speak for the people, and that its own limitations explain the next phase of the struggle.
questions.explanation: The answer must name the social base with instances, show why the narrow base dictated the method, and close with the link to the Assertive and Gandhian phases.
